video_title: How Nations Fumble the Military Tech Race - Dead Ends, Superweapons  & Missing the Moment
gist: Perun uses historical cases (bows to guns, red trousers, Plan Z, V3, the 1957 white paper, EMALS) to show how militaries err by adopting tech too late or too early, framing it as a potential-versus-maturity timing problem. He argues the August 2026 White House order to revert CVN 81 from EMALS to steam ignores maturing reliability data and creates supply-chain uncertainty, and that in the drone age, learning by doing and building industry early may beat a cheaper wait-and-see approach.

themes.theme: Maturity vs potential: timing tech adoption

insights.claim: New military technologies arrive in their least mature, least scaled form, so they often lose head-to-head against incumbent tech on reliability and unit cost even when their long-run potential is higher; the key decision is when to invest heavily, not whether.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Use a potential-vs-maturity lens on any disruptive defense or industrial tech: early underperformance is not proof of a dead end, and incumbency is not proof of durability.
insights.quote: The keyword here to differentiate from potential is maturity.

insights.claim: Solar versus coal is the civilian template: in the early 2000s commercial solar had immature supply chains and high per-unit costs, but because mature technologies improve slowly, photovoltaics became far more efficient over a decade while coal barely improved.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Mature incumbents compound slowly while high-potential entrants ride steep learning curves; the cost crossover is the investable moment.
insights.quote: once a tech is mature, improvements tend to come more slowly than they do in high potential less mature ones

insights.claim: Early adopters buy inferior product: early tanks bought in 1918 were vastly worse than 1928 or 1938 designs (BT-7, Panzer III), and early M16A1s were far less reliable than the 1980s M16A2.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Buying first-generation hardware in bulk without urgent need locks in obsolete inventory; stage procurement during rapid-iteration periods.
insights.quote: Early tanks, for example, were kind of trash.

insights.claim: Transitions often involve long coexistence of old and new tech where everyone expects the switch and only bets on timing; in the 1866 Great Tea Race the clippers Taeping and Ariel finished 28 minutes apart after 99 days, yet a steamship leaving China 8 days after Ariel arrived 15 days earlier, and the Suez Canal sealed steam's advantage.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Peak-performance showcases of a mature incumbent can coincide with its obsolescence; watch infrastructure changes (like a canal) that tilt economics decisively.
insights.quote: the technological writing was on the wall

insights.claim: Resistance to new military tech is driven by career risk aversion and organizational incumbency: senior leaders drawn from dominant combat arms (e.g. cavalryman Douglas Haig, battleship admirals) are biased toward the branches that may be technologically endangered.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Expect budget fights where legacy-branch leadership (e.g. helicopter communities) slows reallocation to drones; procurement inertia can lag technological reality.
insights.quote: how comfortable would you be making that argument to somebody who'd spent 20 or 25 years of their careers in choppers?

insights.claim: Interwar Germany repeated its WWI mistake with Plan Z, prioritising a capital-ship fleet including 10 battleships over U-boats that had actually worked, and lost the early-war window for extra U-boats before belatedly reallocating.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Militaries can over-index on prestige platforms that failed before; flag programs funded on tradition rather than demonstrated combat value.
insights.quote: the German plan put a lot of industrial emphasis stuff that hadn't worked the first time and relatively little on the stuff that did, like the U-boats

insights.claim: France entered 1914 in red trousers despite knowing from the Boer and Balkan Wars that bright uniforms were deadly; political opposition killed reform ('The red pants are France'), yet once war started France quickly switched to horizon blue, proving change was feasible.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Tradition can become a reason in itself, separate from utility; when a fix proves fast in wartime, the prewar delay was a choice, not a constraint.
insights.quote: eliminate the red trousers, never. The red pants are France

insights.claim: Industrial incumbency is a pressure group: firms geared to existing products lobby for more of the same, e.g. makers of big guns and armour plate arguing the navy needs more big guns and armour plate.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Discount incumbent contractors' advocacy against disruptive substitutes; lobbying strength can delay adoption of better tech.
insights.quote: It's not shocking if a company that makes big guns and armored plate argues that what your navy really needs is, would you believe it, even more big guns and armored plate.

insights.claim: Incumbency isn't absolute: a rival can force change (France's 1859 ironclad Gloire triggered Britain's larger HMS Warrior), and leaders can disrupt themselves (Royal Navy's Dreadnought; the US leaping from 4th-gen fighters to stealth and 5th-gen).
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Adversary moves (like the MiG-25 prompting the F-15) can trigger outsized procurement responses that benefit domestic primes.
insights.quote: The point is incumbency is an absolute

themes.theme: EMALS vs steam: US carrier catapult reversal

insights.claim: The Ford-class carrier's EMALS offers higher launch energy, smoother acceleration with less airframe strain, smaller internal volume, and lower manning and maintenance than Nimitz-class steam catapults.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: EMALS is the direction of travel for carrier aviation; suppliers of electromagnetic launch tech hold structural advantage.
insights.quote: It takes up significantly less volume within a ship because you don't need all that complex steam architecture now

insights.claim: EMALS reliability matured sharply: 201 failures in 1,967 test launches (about 10%) in 2013; 181 mean cycles between operational mission failure per a January 2021 report; 460 in FY21 and 614 in FY22.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Early reliability critiques can become stale; track the trend line of mean cycles between failures rather than early test results.
insights.quote: 201 test failures out of 1,967 test launches, a dismal 10% failure rate

insights.claim: In 2026 the Ford generated combat sorties in the war with Iran (earning its strike group a presidential unit citation), and the CNO reported Ford sortie generation at 120 to 130% of the Nimitz class.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Hard combat and test data now validate EMALS, undermining the case for reverting to steam.
insights.quote: between 120 to 130% of the Nimitz class on sortie generation rate

insights.claim: Other carrier powers are betting on electromagnetic catapults: China's Fujian is the only EMALS-equipped conventionally powered carrier, India is reportedly considering them, and France ordered EMALS from General Atomics for its France Libre super carrier due in the 2030s.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: General Atomics has export demand for EMALS independent of US policy; global consensus favors electromagnetic launch.
insights.quote: They're going with the American option, ordering their emails from General Atomics in the United States

insights.claim: An August 2026 White House national security memorandum on rebuilding the Navy and shipbuilding base ordered a plan within 60 days to replace EMALS and advanced weapon elevators with steam and hydraulic systems on CVN 81, contradicting its own instruction elsewhere to stop iterative design changes.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Policy risk: a politically driven redesign of a carrier already under construction; watch for the plan's outcome and any congressional pushback.
insights.quote: the required measures to replace the electromagnetic aircraft launch systems and advanced weapon elevators with steam and hydraulic systems for the construction of CVN 81

insights.claim: Trump has been skeptical of EMALS since at least 2017-2018, saying you need to be Albert Einstein to work it, while the Navy captain he asked recommended electromagnetic catapults.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The steam reversion reflects long-held presidential preference rather than new technical evidence.
insights.quote: you have to be Albert Einstein to work it properly

insights.claim: CVN 81 is already under construction and behind schedule (now expected 2034 instead of 2032); retrofitting steam catapults after steel has been cut is very unlikely to speed delivery, since catapults are not plug-and-play and EMALS's space savings have already been used.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Expect further CVN 81 delays and cost growth if the steam redesign proceeds; carrier-count shortfalls versus congressional mandates could widen.
insights.quote: Cats are not exactly a plug-and-play component.

insights.claim: Reverting to steam would require standing up a second parallel catapult industrial base with weaker economies of scale on obsolescent tech, since the US hasn't built new steam catapults in a long time and still needs EMALS industry for Ford ships and French contracts.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Dual industrial bases raise costs for the Navy and fragment demand for suppliers.
insights.quote: standing up a second parallel industrial base for your carrier catapults

insights.claim: Even if the steam change never happens, policy flip-flopping creates demand-forecasting uncertainty for long-lead suppliers (will it be permanent, will the next administration reverse it), and uncertainty paralyzes investment.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Defense supply chain names exposed to carrier programs face headline risk and capex hesitation; certainty years ahead is what long-lead manufacturers need.
insights.quote: uncertainty when it to investment is a paralytic agent

insights.claim: The memorandum also allows a foreign provider to build up to two ships of a class overseas for the US Navy if it simultaneously builds, buys, or invests in a US shipyard with US workers to build more of the class, and bars iterative changes to mature parent designs.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Opens a path for allied shipbuilders to enter the US naval market via US yard investments; watch foreign yard acquisitions in the US.
insights.quote: the Navy shall not impose iterative design changes upon the original mature parent designs

themes.theme: Betting too early: dead ends and overhype

insights.claim: Technology forecasts err in both directions: naysayers (a 1995 article doubting online shopping and the internet) assume new tech never catches up, while zealots (interwar air-power theorists, monkey-picture NFTs) assume instant total disruption; the truth need not lie in the middle.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Sometimes going all-in is correct (reusable rocketry came to dominate global market share); don't default to a midpoint between bulls and bears.
insights.quote: Sometimes the legitimate bet is to go all in on something like reusable rocketry and then come to dominate global market share.

insights.claim: A technology can be good yet still lose because something better replaces it soon: German WWII rocket fighters outperformed piston fighters but were beaten by maturing jets with afterburners.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Compare a new tech against the next emerging alternative, not just the incumbent.
insights.quote: Rocket motors weren't going to be outcompeted by piston engine fighters, they were going to be beaten by jets.

insights.claim: Intercontinental-range guns are a recurring money sink: the US Army's strategic long-range cannon (1,000+ mile range) faded in favor of truck-launched missiles, and Germany's V3 supergun fired zero rounds at London after 20,000 shells were made that tumbled above 1,000 m/s versus a design speed of 1,500.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of programs that try to make guns do missile jobs; missiles on trucks tend to win.
insights.quote: people who try and make guns do missile things

insights.claim: The V3 was redundant (the V2 already offered near-uninterceptable strikes on London) and ignored that allied air superiority, the reason for vengeance weapons, also made the fixed site vulnerable; Lancasters bombed it with earthquake bombs, making it a net negative.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Check whether a new program duplicates existing capability and whether its own assumptions (e.g. adversary air superiority) undermine it.
insights.quote: the Germans discovered the peril of skipping test day

insights.claim: The US Army's Pentomic Division correctly predicted nuclear weapons would grow but misread how nukes would actually be used, optimising for a nuclear battlefield at the expense of the conventional wars it actually fought.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Right technology call plus wrong battlefield framing still loses; stress-test geopolitical assumptions behind force design.

insights.claim: Britain's 1957 defence white paper bet that surface-to-air missiles would replace manned fighters and halted advanced fighter work beyond the P.1; the call was quickly reversed, but too late for significant parts of the UK aviation industrial base.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Over-hyped substitution forecasts can permanently damage an industrial base; a reversal does not restore lost capacity.
insights.quote: the RAF are unlikely to have a requirement for fighter aircraft of types more advanced than the supersonic P 1

insights.claim: The early F-4 Phantom dropped the internal gun on the expectation missiles would dominate; the E model reintroduced it, and the USAF has since kept cannons on the F-22 and F-35A, while the PRC omits them on designs like the J-20.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Missiles did win long-term, but scrapping the legacy capability too early cost effectiveness; hedge with legacy systems during transitions.

insights.claim: Lasers and directed energy are like fusion power, always a couple of decades away; the airborne laser on a 747 was operationally impractical and cancelled, and only in the 2020s are lasers deployed on warships or for base defense, still immature for larger threats, longer ranges, or armored vehicles.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Directed-energy investment is justified for counter-drone roles today, but overinvesting at the expense of legacy air defense remains risky.
insights.quote: incredibly high in potential, yet somehow always a couple of decades away

themes.theme: Second-mover advantage vs learning by doing in the drone age

insights.claim: There is a genuine second-mover advantage when the question is when, not what: waiting lets you skip immature designs, and copying is cheaper than pioneering, as the Soviets did by buying Rolls-Royce Nene engines and reverse-engineering them into the RD-45 and Klimov VK-1.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Fast followers can catch up cheaply once a leader proves the tech; export and tech-transfer decisions can erode a lead.
insights.quote: copying someone else's answer once they've done the work often the path of least resistance

insights.claim: Russia and Ukraine iterate drones so fast that 2022 designs would need full replacement by 2026; that is little waste for them because they burn through drones constantly, but peacetime militaries fear stocking obsolete drones, justifying cautious procurement.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Peacetime drone buyers will favor smaller, staged orders and rapid refresh cycles over large bulk buys of current designs.
insights.quote: If you'd gone all in on Russian and Ukrainian drone designs from 2022, by 2026, you'd be looking to replace them all.

insights.claim: Contrary to the wait-and-see camp, technological maturity is not passive: using immature tech builds military expertise, TTPs, and an industrial workforce that feeds back into development, so procuring early can position a country to scale fast when the tech becomes decisive.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Countries and firms that build drone industrial capacity and doctrine now may gain durable advantage; underinvestment risks compounding strategic and economic gaps.
insights.quote: it might make sense to start procuring it, building up the industry, and incorporating it into the force before you actually reach that point

insights.claim: Ukraine and Russia hold a massive drone advantage because they built the industry, workforce, TTPs, and experienced personnel from 2021-2023 onward, even if they spent heavily on early designs.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The drone industrial and doctrinal lead sits with the belligerents; other nations will be catching up through late 2026 into 2027.
insights.quote: they've been the ones developing the industry, the workforce, the TTPs, and the experienced personnel

insights.claim: In late 2026 into 2027, nations face rapid evolution in drones, unmanned systems, communications, and AI, with many advocates incentivized to claim their idea is the next gunpowder; sitting still is not an option, and who got it right may not be clear until the 2030s or actual combat.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Expect noisy, hype-driven defense-tech procurement; favor approaches that experiment smart and fail safe over all-in bets.
insights.quote: develop efficiently and fast, experiment smart, and fail safe
